cards.text: Hezekiah, king of Judah, was sick enough to die, and the LORD added fifteen years to his life (Isaiah 38:1-9). The news travels all the way to Babylon, where King Merodach-baladan son of Baladan hears about the illness AND the recovery. Friend, when a king that far away hears you got better, you KNOW it was a big deal.

cards.question: So what does Merodach-baladan, king of Babylon, send to Hezekiah?

cards.text: A get-well card from a KING! The envoys arrive from Babylon, and Hezekiah welcomes them gladly.

cards.question: Hezekiah keeps his armory and storehouses closed and shows the envoys from Babylon only a few of his treasures.

cards.text: Silver, gold, spices, precious oil, the ENTIRE armory: there's nothing in his palace or in all his dominion that Hezekiah doesn't show them. Friend, that's not a tour, that's handing a stranger your unlocked phone with the banking app already open.
Then the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz (Isaiah 38:1) goes to King Hezekiah. He asks where those men came from and what they said.

cards.question: When the prophet Isaiah asks where the envoys came from, Hezekiah refuses to tell him.

cards.text: Hezekiah tells him they came from a distant land, from Babylon. Then Isaiah asks what they've seen, and Hezekiah answers, "They have seen everything in my palace."

cards.question: Isaiah brings Hezekiah the word of the LORD of Hosts. The time will surely come when everything in Hezekiah's palace, and all that his fathers stored up, will be what?
The LORD says Babylon will carry off most of Hezekiah's treasure, but a little will be left in the palace.
It's not just the treasure. The LORD says some of Hezekiah's ___ will be taken away to be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.

cards.text: His own flesh and blood. That's heavy news, and now it's Hezekiah's turn to answer the prophet.

cards.question: What does Hezekiah tell Isaiah about the word of the LORD he just heard?
Hezekiah calls the word of the LORD good. What was he thinking?

answers.text: At least his own lifetime will have peace
Babylon will soon forget all about Judah
Isaiah could still turn out to be mistaken

cards.text: He thought, "At least there will be peace and security in my lifetime." I've done that with a messy oven, friend: "Tomorrow Dorin can handle it," and Tomorrow Dorin is NEVER happy with me.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 8 quotes "They have seen everything in my palace.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The last story card adds nothing new. Card 14's right answer already covered Hezekiah's thought ('At least his own lifetime will have peace', Isaiah 39:8). Card 15 restates that same thought and adds a joke, so it works as a recap and doesn't move the passage forward. Either cut the card or end on a beat that hasn't been told yet. For example, the quote could move to a story card before card 14 and card 14 could ask something else, or the joke could ride on card 12.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage. No recap cards.

findings.problem: The joke on the opening card ('when a king that far away hears you got better, you KNOW it was a big deal') is mild and pleasant rather than laugh-out-loud funny. It reads like a nice dad being agreeable, not like Papa Dorin's Katt Williams, Chappelle or Kevin Hart energy.

rule.text: Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
